title: Prayers for others
hookLine: blessings for the sick, the community and the country

lines: A NAME WHISPERED TO THE LEADER.
A LIST ON A SCRAP OF PAPER.
cards: While the Torah lies open on the table, there's a pause between readings. Someone walks up to the leader and whispers a name. Then another.
Then a list on a scrap of paper. A neighbor's husband after surgery. A cousin's newborn.
A friend in rehab. The leader starts a short prayer, and when it reaches the gap, the names pour in, sometimes for a full minute.
In some congregations, people simply stand and say them aloud, one after another, until the room goes quiet again.

teach.h: MAY THE ONE WHO BLESSED OUR ANCESTORS.
teach.b: The prayer begins Mi sheberach avoteinu: may the One who blessed our ancestors, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and in many communities Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah, bless this person.
It's a frame, and almost anything can go in it.

teach.h: FOR THE SICK, THE CALLED UP, THE NEW.
teach.b: There's a Mi Sheberach for each person called up to the Torah. One for the sick, asking for complete healing of body and spirit, where the names from that scrap of paper go.
One for the whole congregation and everyone who gives to it and serves it. One for a new baby, one for a couple about to marry.
Many synagogues also pray for the country and its leaders, and in many communities for the State of Israel and those who defend it. Praying for the government has deep roots.

teach.h: SEEK THE PEACE OF THE CITY.
teach.b: The prophet Jeremiah writes to the exiles in Babylon, in the old Jewish translation: "seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray unto the LORD for it; for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace."
Not Jerusalem, the city they lost. Babylon, the city that took them captive.
In Pirkei Avot, Rabbi Chanina, deputy of the priests, says to pray for the welfare of the government, because without it, people would swallow one another alive.
In recent decades the songwriter Debbie Friedman wrote a sung version of the prayer for healing, and some synagogues now sing it instead.
The frame stays the same: the blessing that reached our ancestors, asked for someone else.

how: During the Torah service, Mi Sheberach blessings are said for those called up, for the sick, whose names are added aloud or whispered to the leader, and for the congregation; many synagogues also say prayers for the country and for the State of Israel.

o: a blessing for the bread at the Sabbath meal
a prayer of mourning said at the graveside

it's a frame: for those called up, the sick, the congregation, a baby, a couple.
Jeremiah told exiles to pray for the city of their captors

games.q: you're an exile in Babylon. a letter arrives from the prophet Jeremiah. what does it tell you to do about Babylon?
o: curse it and wait to leave.
seek its peace and pray for it.
ignore it and keep to yourselves.
games.why: seek the peace of the city, and pray unto the LORD for it; for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.

practice: Picture the place you live: the main street, the school, the hospital, the people you pass without knowing their names, and the people who run it, the ones you voted for and the ones you didn't.
Hold one wish for the whole place, safety, fairness, enough. If you pray, ask for its peace; if not, just let yourself care, for a minute, about people you'll never meet.
